summary:
The criminal-law layer is unsettled. Sodomy and "unnatural sexual offences" appeared as grounds in the Immigration Act until the High Court of Windhoek declared those references unconstitutional and invalid on 21 June 2024; the government appealed in July 2024. The colonial-era sodomy offence itself remained on the statute book and was not believed to have been used since independence in 1990, and the government told the UN Human Rights Committee it had no intention of repealing it. A December 2024 UNDP review records that Namibia's courts decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2024 and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, while noting that implementation remains contested.

Public displays of affection between two men can still be treated as "immoral" behaviour punishable under the Combating of Immoral Practices Act of 1980.

Partner recognition is the sharpest exposure. On 16 May 2023 the Supreme Court ruled that same-sex marriages performed abroad must be recognised under the Immigration Act, giving non-Namibian spouses the same residence rights as opposite-sex spouses. Compliance has not followed: immigration officials told litigant Daniel Digashu that the ruling covers only the couples who brought the case, and he is issued a visitor's visa on every exit from the country. Gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than to "all persons". In December 2024 parliament passed an act explicitly forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad, overriding the 2023 judgment. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law cannot rely on the 2023 ruling to secure a spouse's residence rights.

Earlier residence litigation produced the same individualised outcomes. In 2001 a Namibian woman's German wife, Elisabeth Frank, won a Supreme Court permanent residence permit without the court endorsing same-sex relationships, and in January 2018 Daniel Digashu won a court petition to enter Namibia while his case was reviewed.

Article 10 of the constitution does not list gender identity or sexual orientation. A 2017 analysis by the Southern Africa Litigation Centre argues that "other status" should be read to include them, following the UN Human Rights Committee's position.

Health care is governed by professional rules that bar discrimination. Health professionals are bound by the Ethical Guidelines for Health Professionals (2010, Health Professions Councils of Namibia), whose Sections 2.1.5, 2.6 and 3.2.2 require that personal beliefs not prejudice patient care and prohibit discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, and the Ministry of Health and Social Services' Patient Charter makes "Impartiality" a core value requiring equal treatment irrespective of sex, gender and sexuality. Against that, the 2009 ministry regulations on scope of practice for clinical and educational psychologists still treat "sexual and gender identity" as disorders.

Media regulation offers a limited protection. The Broadcasting Code for Broadcasting Licensees 2018 (General Notice No. 602) bars licensees from broadcasting material that advocates hatred based on gender or sexual orientation, sanctions violence or unlawful conduct on those grounds, and prohibits material likely to incite hatred or severe ridicule against persons because of sexual orientation where that constitutes incitement to harm (Sections 5, 7(2), 7(3)). The UN Human Rights Committee recommended in 2016 that Namibia legislate against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Public assembly by LGBT people has proceeded without government impediment. OutRight Namibia organised the country's first pride parades: the Windhoek march of December 2013 drew about 100 people, around 200 marched in June 2017, and hundreds marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund in December 2018. The first Namibian Lesbian Festival was held in Windhoek in November 2017, bringing more than sixty young lesbians from eight regions together for a week of public poetry, story, music, drama and dance, and was repeated in November 2018.
tangentialFactors:
Political hostility to LGBT rights is organised rather than incidental. In June 2014 a Namibian party modelled on South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original. The SWAPO Party Youth League is listed among parties opposing LGBTQ rights.

The op-ed by Daniel Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre attributes part of the compliance failure to reporting that amplified the non-implementation, alongside a hostile parliamentary response of marriage bills.

Namibia sits inside the African Commission's Resolution 275 framework on LGBT rights, which the December 2024 UNDP review treats as the regional reference point for the country's decriminalisation and residency-recognition developments.
localsOnly:
Gender-marker changes are available under section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 on medical evidence, handled case by case; the Legal Assistance Centre described the process in 2015 as not problematic.

Resident health and support infrastructure is thin but present. OutRight Namibia opened the country's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May 2018 at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West, offering HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, and mental and sexual and reproductive health services, with plans to add legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. The Namibian Gays and Lesbian Movement runs educational programmes to raise awareness among LGBTQ Namibians, and MPower Community Trust provides sexual health awareness for gay and bisexual men.
outOfScopeNotes:
The government's July 2024 appeal against the High Court of Windhoek's 21 June 2024 ruling on the Immigration Act references has no recorded outcome in the sources reviewed; whether those references are currently enforceable is unresolved.

How the December 2024 act forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad operates against the 16 May 2023 Supreme Court judgment in practice is not sourced beyond the fact of its passage.

The 2017 Southern Africa Litigation Centre analysis of Article 10 and section 7B predates the 2023 marriage-recognition judgment and the 2024 decriminalisation ruling and has not been updated in the material reviewed.

The 2018 account of the sodomy offence being unused since independence is dated and rests on the absence of known prosecutions rather than a formal assurance.
